preamble.summary: LXX Micah is the source of the Bethlehem prophecy that Matthew 2:6 cites to identify Jesus' birthplace, one of the cornerstone passages for Christian Messianic exegesis of the prophets. Micah 7:6 is also quoted by Jesus at Matthew 10:35–36 and Luke 12:53 to describe the household-dividing effect of discipleship. Micah 6:8's ethical summary ('act justly, love mercy, walk humbly') entered Christian moral discourse in its LXX form.
preamble.notable_variants: Matthew 2:6's citation of Micah 5:2 differs from both MT and standard LXX, representing a free composite citation or a Greek Vorlage no longer extant; Micah 6:8's threefold ethical summary in its LXX form as the paradigm of prophetic ethics; Micah 7:6's family-division oracle in its LXX form as the template for Jesus' sayings about discipleship's cost.
preamble.theological_legacy: Matthew 2:6's Micah quotation — placed on the lips of the chief priests and scribes answering Herod — is one of the most consequential single citations in the Gospel of Matthew: it authorizes the claim that Jesus of Nazareth, actually born in Bethlehem, fulfills the Davidic-shepherd prophecy.

renderings.mt_reading: וְאַתָּה בֵּית־לֶחֶם אֶפְרָתָה צָעִיר לִהְיוֹת בְּאַלְפֵי יְהוּדָה
renderings.lxx_reading: καὶ σύ Βηθλεεμ οἶκος τοῦ Εφραθα ὀλιγοστὸς εἶ τοῦ εἶναι ἐν χιλιάσιν Ιουδα
renderings.mt_rendering: But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, though you are small among the clans of Judah
renderings.lxx_rendering: And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephratha, are few in number to be among the thousands of Judah
notes: Matthew 2:6 cites this verse, but with a striking adjustment: where LXX reads oligostos ei ('you are little'), Matthew reads oudamōs elachistē ei ('by no means are you least'). Matthew inverts the prophecy — no longer 'you are little' but 'you are by no means least.'

The inversion is not a text-critical variant but a homiletic move: the evangelist (or a tradition he inherits) reads the prophecy in light of its fulfillment — Bethlehem's smallness has been exalted by the birth of the Messiah.

Matthew also replaces 'clans' (chiliasin, 'thousands') with hēgemosin ('rulers') and adds 'who will shepherd my people Israel' from 2 Samuel 5:2 — a combined citation typical of early Christian and rabbinic anthological method. The LXX Micah 5:2 supplies the textual starting point for this fused Messianic citation.

renderings.mt_reading: עֲשׂוֹת מִשְׁפָּט וְאַהֲבַת חֶסֶד וְהַצְנֵעַ לֶכֶת עִם־אֱלֹהֶיךָ
renderings.lxx_reading: ποιεῖν κρίμα καὶ ἀγαπᾶν ἔλεος καὶ ἕτοιμον εἶναι τοῦ πορεύεσθαι μετὰ κυρίου θεοῦ σου
renderings.mt_rendering: Only to act justly, to love faithful love, and to walk humbly with your God
renderings.lxx_rendering: To do justice and to love mercy, and to be ready to walk with the Lord your God
notes: The threefold ethical summary of Micah 6:8 is rendered in LXX with krima (justice), eleos (mercy), and poreuesthai meta kyriou (walking with the Lord).

The LXX renders hatsnea lekhet ('walk humbly') as hetoimon einai tou poreuesthai ('be ready to walk') — a softening of the Hebrew's 'humbly' into 'readiness.' Some interpreters see this as a Hellenistic Jewish piety-move; others note the Hebrew is itself debated.

Matthew 23:23 (weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faithfulness) appears to allude to Micah 6:8's threefold summary using its LXX vocabulary of krisis (judgment/justice), eleos, and pistis (faithfulness/faith).

renderings.mt_rendering: For a son dishonors his father … a person's enemies are the members of their own household
renderings.lxx_rendering: For a son dishonors his father … a man's enemies are those of his own house
notes: Matthew 10:35–36 and Luke 12:53 both cite this verse as Jesus describes the household-rending effect of discipleship: 'I have come to set a man against his father … and a man's enemies will be those of his own household.'
The LXX's exact wording — echtroi tou anthrōpou hoi andres tou oikou autou ('a man's enemies are the men of his own house') — is what Matthew 10:36 quotes.

Jesus' selection of Micah 7:6 as a scriptural warrant for the disruptive character of messianic allegiance is typical of his rhetorical method: take a prophetic text lamenting social decay and press it as a prophecy being fulfilled in the Kingdom's arrival.
